  fromJSON(paste(txt, collapse = "\n"), simplifyVector = FALSE)
}

  s <- gsub("&", "and", as.character(arg0_s), fixed = TRUE)
  s <- gsub("_", " ", s, fixed = TRUE)
  trimws(s)
}

fmt_yr <- function (arg0_y) {
  y <- as.numeric(arg0_y)
  if (y < 0) return(paste0(abs(round(y)), "BC"))
  return(paste0(round(y), "AD"))
}

# Abstract

Peninsular South Asia south of the Krishna and Tungabhadra basins constitutes an ecologically distinct subcontinent comprising 167.458 km² of land across Tamil Nadu and Kerala, partitioned into 1.989 terrestrial cells on a 5-arcminute grid. Framed by the Western Ghats mountain barrier, the Arabian Sea, the Indian Ocean and the Bay of Bengal, this territory sustained a demographic evolution distinct from the alluvial plains of northern India. Across ten millennia from 10000BC to 300AD, regional population expanded from 35k terminal Pleistocene foragers following initial post-glacial recolonisation to 120k in 5000BC, quickening through the Southern Neolithic and early pastoral phases to reach 480k in 2000BC and 1,15M in 1000BC. During the Early Iron Age Megalithic expansion, communal mortuary architecture, iron metallurgy and tank-irrigated rice agriculture accelerated demographic mass to 2,10M in 500BC and 3,40M in 200BC. At the turn of the common era, as the three crowned monarchies of the Cheras, Cholas and Pandyas established integrated regional polities and opened trans-oceanic maritime commerce across the Indian Ocean to the Mediterranean world, regional population climbed to 4,20M in 0AD, reaching 4,80M in 200AD and culminating at 5,10M in 300AD (yielding an aggregate density of 3.045,54 persons per 100 km²).

Demographic weight was anchored along three physiographic and political provinces. The Kaveri Delta, Tondaimandalam and Kongu Uplands supported 2,24M inhabitants in 300AD (44,0% of regional population; 2.642,11 persons per 100 km²), integrating the agrarian delta capital of Uraiyur and the coastal emporium of Kaveripattinam with the semi-arid mineral uplands of Kodumanal and Kanchipuram. The Vaigai-Thamirabarani Basins and Pandya Heartland housed 1,53M people (30,0%; 3.334,35 persons per 100 km²), anchored by the inland metropolis of Madurai, the industrial craft centre of Keeladi and the pearl fishery port of Korkai. The Chera Coastal Malabar and Western Ghats Littoral accommodated 1,33M inhabitants (26,0%; 3.618,99 persons per 100 km²), where high-precipitation rainforest coastal strips, maritime lagoons and the Palghat Gap gapway linked the spice emporium of Pattanam with the interior Kongu corridor.

This quantitative demographic reconstruction integrates 1.579 catalogued settlements (842 in the Kaveri Delta and Tondaimandalam sub-region, 457 in the Vaigai-Thamirabarani Pandya heartland and 280 in Chera Malabar) with systematic archaeological survey gazetteers, radiocarbon-calibrated stratigraphy, archaeobotanical flotation sequences and four-wave source ledger saturation audits [@Champakalakshmi1996Trade; @Allchin1995Archaeology]. Evaluated across the full gazetteer, the settlement hierarchy conforms to a Zipf rank-size distribution ($\alpha = 0,94$, $R^2 = 0,95$). By isolating nucleated urban centres from dasymetrically distributed rural cultivators, the study shows that Early Historic Tamilakam achieved substantial urbanisation without reproducing northern monarchical bureaucratic centralisation, instead drawing demographic cohesion from lineage-based pastoral-agrarian clans, craft guilds and maritime trade networks.

# Background

## Environmental Geography and Fluvial Drainage

The physical architecture of southern peninsular India is governed by the structural divide of the Western Ghats (Sahyadri), a crystalline fault-scarp mountain chain rising over 2.000 metres above sea level [@Ponton2012Aridificat; @Rick2022Coring]. The Western Ghats intercept the southwest summer monsoon between June and September, depositing intense precipitation exceeding 3.000 mm annually along the Malabar coastal shelf while casting a pronounced rain shadow across the eastern tablelands of Tamil Nadu, where annual rainfall drops to 600 mm to 900 mm [@Ponton2012Aridificat]. The eastern plains receive their primary moisture from the northeast retreat monsoon between October and December, creating an asymmetrical bi-monsoonal hydrological regime that demanded distinct water-harvesting strategies across the peninsula.

The drainage network mirrors this topographic asymmetry. Three major river basins flow eastward across Tamil Nadu into the Bay of Bengal [@KingwellBanham2019Rainfed]:
1. The Kaveri River, originating in the Brahmagiri Hills of Kodagu, traverses the southern Deccan plateau before dropping through the Hogenakkal Falls and entering the broad plains of Tamil Nadu. Joined by the Bhavani, Noyyal and Amaravathi tributaries in the Kongu region, the Kaveri forms an expansive fan-shaped delta east of Tiruchirappalli, depositing fertile alluvial silts that supported the densest agrarian populations of southern India.
2. The Vaigai River, draining the Varushanad and Andipatti hills, flows southeast past Madurai through semi-arid plains before discharging into the Palk Strait near Ramanathapuram. Though ephemeral in its lower reaches, its waters were harnessed through elaborate chains of irrigation tanks (*eris*).
3. The Thamirabarani River, rising in the Agasthyamalai range of the southern Western Ghats, represents the only perennial river system in southern Tamil Nadu, fed by both monsoons and supplying fertile silts to the Tirunelveli and Thoothukudi plains.

To the west of the mountains lies the narrow coastal littoral of Kerala, extending 580 km from Kasaragod to Cape Comorin. Dissected by 41 westward-flowing rivers, of which the Periyar, Bharathapuzha and Pamba are preeminent, the Malabar plain features interconnected brackish lagoons (*kayals*), barrier beaches and lateritic foothill terraces. Communication between the western and eastern slopes of the peninsula was channelled through structural mountain passes, chief among them the 30 km wide Palghat Gap (Palakkad Gap) between the Nilgiris and the Anaimalai Hills, which operated as an overland demographic and commercial conduit linking the Malabar port of Muziris directly with the Kongu iron and gem-working centres [@Abraham2003Chera; @Kelly2024Report].

## Mesolithic Foragers and Microlithic Dune Traditions

Human occupation of southern peninsular India extends into the middle and late Pleistocene, documented by Lower and Middle Palaeolithic handaxe assemblages at Attirampakkam in the Kortallaiyar river valley of northern Tamil Nadu [@Biswas2022Founder]. Following the Last Glacial Maximum, terminal Pleistocene and early Holocene hunter-gatherer communities adapted to transforming climatic and vegetational conditions through intensive microlithic technologies [@Rick2022Coring]. Regional population stood at 35k in 10000BC, yielding a low aggregate density of 20,90 persons per 100 km².

Mesolithic occupation left dense surface scatters across distinctive geological formations [@Tacon2010Rock]:
- The coastal red sand dunes (*teri* sites) of Thoothukudi and Tirunelveli districts, where windblown quartz sand formations preserved geometric microliths (backed blades, lunates, trapezes, scrapers) fabricated from chert, quartz and chalcedony. These communities exploited maritime littoral resources, estuarine molluscs and terrestrial game [@Rick2022Coring].
- Rock shelters and granite inselbergs in the Dharmapuri, Krishnagiri and Salem districts, where microlithic tool manufacture was accompanied by prehistoric rock paintings depicting wild fauna (deer, nilgai, wild boars) and hunting groups [@Tacon2010Rock].
- Highland rainforest foraging adaptations in the Western Ghats, where mobile bands exploited wild yams, tubers, small game and honey, initiating subsistence modes that persisted among indigenous forest communities such as the Paliyars into historic centuries [@Selvakumar2018Paliyars].

Between 10000BC and 5000BC, regional foraging populations expanded gradually from 35k to 120k, accompanied by broadened subsistence broad-spectrum foraging and seasonal mobility between upland game tracks and coastal lagoons [@Rick2022Coring; @Das2016Tracing].

## Southern Neolithic Pastoralism and Iron Age Megalithic Emergence

During the third and second millennia BC, food production became established across the interior plateaus of peninsular India [@Roberts2015Local; @Johansen2023Social]. The Southern Neolithic complex, characterised by pastoral ash-mounds, polished stone celts and handmade burnished grey pottery, extended southward from the Raichur and Bellary doabs into the Dharmapuri, Krishnagiri and North Arcot districts of Tamil Nadu [@Venkatasubbaiah2022Protohisto; @Saraswat1991Archaeobot]. Archaeobotanical and faunal investigations demonstrate an economy anchored by humped zebu cattle (*Bos indicus*), alongside domestic sheep, goats, indigenous browntop millet (*Brachiaria ramosa*), bristly foxtail millet (*Setaria verticillata*), horsegram (*Macrotyloma uniflorum*) and green gram (*Vigna radiata*) [@Fuller2020Chapter; @Roberts2015Local]. Regional population reached 480k by 2000BC.

From roughly 1200BC to 1000BC, peninsular India transitioned into the Early Iron Age, marked by the rapid adoption of iron smelting and the construction of monumental mortuary monuments known collectively as the Megalithic complex [@K2014Early; @Rao1989South]. Regional population expanded to 1,15M in 1000BC and 2,10M by 500BC, reflecting fundamental technological and agrarian transformations [@Wunderlich2019Hierarchy]:
1. Megalithic architecture assumed diverse regional typologies across Tamil Nadu and Kerala [@Rao1989South; @Pinky2026Megaliths]:
   - Dolmenoid cists and port-holed stone cists enclosed by granite stone circles in the Kongu and Tondaimandalam uplands.
   - Rock-cut burial caves (*kudaikallu*) and umbrella stones (*topikallu*) excavated into lateritic bedrock across the Malabar littoral of Kerala.
   - Massive urn burial fields (*mudumakkal thazhi*) in the Thamirabarani and Vaigai basins, preeminently at Adichanallur, where thousands of pyriform terracotta urns containing excarnated skeletal remains, iron weapons, bronze vessels and gold diadems were interred along gravel river terraces [@MushrifTripathy2019Tales].
   - Menhirs and dolmens erected on high ridge saddles in the Nilgiris and Anaimalai mountains [@Simone2021Grave].
2. High-carbon wootz steel metallurgy developed rapidly in the Kongu uplands, notably at Kodumanal along the Noyyal River, where crucibles, furnaces and iron slag confirm large-scale production of steel blades, agricultural iron shares, hoes and chisels [@Abraham2003Chera].
3. The expansion of wet-rice cultivation (*Oryza sativa*) transformed low-lying alluvial basins [@KingwellBanham2019Rainfed]. Iron implements enabled the clearing of dense tropical vegetation and the construction of contour earthen bunds to trap monsoon run-off, creating tank-irrigated paddy landscapes that supported permanent, high-density village aggregates.

## Early Historic Urbanism, Sangam Literature and Trans-Oceanic Commerce

Between 500BC and 300AD, Tamil Nadu and Kerala coalesced into the socio-political formation known in classical Tamil bardic literature as Tamilakam [@Monsingh2025Ancient; @Abraham2003Chera]. The region was presided over by the three crowned monarchs (*muventhar*): the Cheras in the west (Malabar, Palghat Gap and central Kerala, capital at Karur and port at Muziris), the Cholas in the Kaveri heartland (central delta, capital at Uraiyur and port at Kaveripattinam/Puhar), and the Pandyas in the south (Vaigai and Thamirabarani basins, capital at Madurai and port at Korkai) [@Abraham2003Chera; @Dwivedi2021Political]. Peripheral tracts were governed by minor chieftaincies (*velir*), who controlled upland hill territories and forest resources.

Classical Sangam poetry, compiled in the *Ettuthogai* (Eight Anthologies) and *Pattupattu* (Ten Idylls), describes a landscape categorised into five physiographic-ecological zones (*tinai*): *kurinji* (mountainous hunting and honey-gathering tracts), *mullai* (pastoral scrublands), *marutham* (irrigated alluvial agricultural valleys), *neithal* (coastal littoral and fishing margins), and *palai* (arid wastelands) [@Monsingh2025Ancient]. This conceptual schema reflected genuine economic specialisation and symbiotic inter-zonal exchange, where upland spices and timber were traded for deltaic rice, salt and coastal dried fish.

Urbanisation took root at major nodes [@Dwivedi2019Early; @Champakalakshmi1996Trade; @Allchin1995Archaeology]:
- Madurai, established along the Vaigai River, expanded into a planned urban capital accommodating 30,8k inhabitants in 200BC, 42,7k in 0AD and a peak of 48k in 100AD, protected by moats and ramparts and celebrated as the seat of the Tamil literary academies (*sangams*).
- Keeladi, situated 12 km southeast of Madurai, revealed an extensive urban crafting settlement reaching 11k inhabitants in 100BC, with brick structures, covered drainage canals, terracotta ring-wells, weaving vats and Tamil-Brahmi inscribed potsherds dating from the sixth century BC onward [@Baskar2026Regional; @Rao1985Indian].
- Kaveripattinam (Puhar), situated at the Kaveri estuary, became a cosmopolitan harbour town housing 34,3k inhabitants in 0AD and peaking at 45k in 200AD, featuring brick warehouses, wharves and residential sectors described in the *Silappadikaram*.
- Uraiyur (modern Tiruchirappalli), commanding the apex of the Kaveri delta, formed a dense textile-weaving and administrative metropolis housing 32k residents in 0AD and peaking at 36k in 200AD.
- Kanchipuram on the Palar River operated as the northern commercial and religious capital of Tondaimandalam, housing 30k people in 0AD and expanding to 42,7k by 300AD.

Simultaneously, the discovery of monsoon wind navigation across the Arabian Sea linked Tamilakam directly with the Red Sea ports of Roman Egypt (Myos Hormos, Berenike) and the Mediterranean economy [@Tomber2009Migration; @Cobb2023Indian; @Abraham2023Recent]. At Pattanam (Muziris) on the Periyar delta, excavations exposed brick quays, a dugout canoe, Roman amphora fragments, terra sigillata, glass beads and semi-precious stone debitage [@Kelly2024Report]. At Arikamedu near Puducherry, brick dyeing vats and Roman pottery confirm intensive industrial manufacturing for international export [@Deshpande1975Indian; @Dwivedi2021Tools]. Korkai and Alagankulam dominated the Gulf of Mannar pearl fishery and maritime traffic with Sri Lanka [@Dissanayake2022Megalithic; @Thapar1979Indian].

# Methodology

## Spatial Disaggregation and Environmental Covariates

To model demographic densities across 167.458 km² of land area, the INDUS spatial engine partitions Tamil Nadu and Kerala into 1.989 active 5-arcminute grid cells (each approximately 9,2 km by 9,2 km at tropical latitudes between 8° N and 14° N). Terrestrial cells are calibrated against environmental suitability covariates:
- Fluvial proximity and irrigation suitability: distance decay functions calibrated to perennial rivers (Kaveri, Thamirabarani, Periyar, Bharathapuzha) and seasonal streams (Vaigai, Palar, Ponnaiyar). Cells intersecting alluvial floodplains receive high agricultural weightings [@KingwellBanham2019Rainfed].
- Monsoon precipitation and catchment runoff: spatial weighting based on bi-monsoonal precipitation gradients, separating the high-rainfall western littoral from rain-shadow tank-irrigated eastern plains [@Ponton2012Aridificat].
- Topographic elevation and slope penalties: steep slopes across the Western Ghats (Nilgiris, Anaimalai, Palani, Cardamom hills) and Eastern Ghats outliers receive negative weighting for sedentary farming while retaining modest carry capacities for foraging and pastoralism [@Selvakumar2018Paliyars; @Simone2021Grave].
- Coastal and estuarine access: maritime buffers reflecting accessibility to coastal lagoons, natural harbours and pearl oyster banks along the Gulf of Mannar [@Tomber2009Migration; @Cobb2023Indian].

## Settlement Subtraction and Rural Allocation

To prevent demographic double counting between nucleated urban populations and rural cultivators, 1.579 catalogued settlements with chronological population series are directly anchored to their WGS84 geographic coordinates. These trajectories are grounded in primary historical monographs [@Champakalakshmi1996Trade; @Allchin1995Archaeology; @Erdosy1988Urbanisation], multi-repository archaeological corpora, Census of India Table A-04 and colonial gazetteer baselines [@ImperialGazetteer1908], and macro-envelope *nadu* and *qasba* territorial continuity with strict foundation-year filtering. At each benchmark year, the active population of catalogued settlements within each sub-region is aggregated and subtracted from the sub-regional demographic envelope.

The residual rural population is then allocated across non-settled terrestrial cells according to local environmental suitability indices. A two-pass boundary smoothing algorithm prevents sharp density cliffs across sub-regional borders while preserving authentic topographic boundaries along mountain crests.

## Demographic Uncertainty Envelopes

Every sub-regional and regional benchmark estimate carries an explicit symmetric uncertainty bound (+/- 8% across all benchmark years from 10000BC to 300AD). In 300AD, the regional population of 5,10M is bounded between 4,69M and 5,51M inhabitants. This uncertainty envelope accommodates archaeological variability in urban mound extent, house-floor surface multipliers and seasonal agrarian mobility [@Roberts2015Local; @Rao1989South].

Table \ref{tab:subregions} documents the three physiographic and historical sub-regions, land areas, benchmark populations and 300AD densities.

```{r tbl-subregions, results='asis'}
sub_rows <- lapply(reg_keys, function (rk) {
  r <- mod_data$regions[[rk]]
  a <- as.numeric(r$area_km2)
  p_10k <- as.numeric(r$population[["-10000"]])
  p_5k <- as.numeric(r$population[["-5000"]])
  p_2k <- as.numeric(r$population[["-2000"]])
  p_1k <- as.numeric(r$population[["-1000"]])
  p_500 <- as.numeric(r$population[["-500"]])
  p_200 <- as.numeric(r$population[["-200"]])
  p_0 <- as.numeric(r$population[["0"]])
  p_300 <- as.numeric(r$population[["300"]])
  dens_300 <- p_300 / a * 100
  data.frame(
    Region = if (!is.null(reg_short[[rk]])) reg_short[[rk]] else clean_text(r$name),
    Area = paste0(viscount_fmt_number(a, 0L), " (", viscount_fmt_number(a / tot_area * 100, 1L), "%)"),
    P10000BC = viscount_fmt_pop(p_10k),
    P5000BC = viscount_fmt_pop(p_5k),
    P2000BC = viscount_fmt_pop(p_2k),
    P1000BC = viscount_fmt_pop(p_1k),
    P500BC = viscount_fmt_pop(p_500),
    P200BC = viscount_fmt_pop(p_200),
    P0AD = viscount_fmt_pop(p_0),
    P300AD = viscount_fmt_pop(p_300),
    Density300 = viscount_fmt_number(dens_300, 2L),
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE
  )
})
df_sub <- do.call(rbind, sub_rows)
df_tot <- data.frame(
  Region = "Regional Total",
  Area = paste0(viscount_fmt_number(tot_area, 0L), " (100%)"),
  P10000BC = viscount_fmt_pop(mod_data$summary$headline_population_by_benchmark[["-10000"]]),
  P5000BC = viscount_fmt_pop(mod_data$summary$headline_population_by_benchmark[["-5000"]]),
  P2000BC = viscount_fmt_pop(mod_data$summary$headline_population_by_benchmark[["-2000"]]),
  P1000BC = viscount_fmt_pop(mod_data$summary$headline_population_by_benchmark[["-1000"]]),
  P500BC = viscount_fmt_pop(mod_data$summary$headline_population_by_benchmark[["-500"]]),
  P200BC = viscount_fmt_pop(mod_data$summary$headline_population_by_benchmark[["-200"]]),
  P0AD = viscount_fmt_pop(tot_0),
  P300AD = viscount_fmt_pop(tot_300),
  Density300 = viscount_fmt_number(tot_300 / tot_area * 100, 2L),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)
df_sub <- rbind(df_sub, df_tot)
viscount_table(
  df_sub,
  "Sub-regional land area, benchmark populations and 300AD density across Tamil Nadu and Kerala.",
  c("Sub-Region", "Area km² (Share)", "10000BC", "5000BC", "2000BC", "1000BC", "500BC", "200BC", "0AD", "300AD", "300AD Density"),
  list(label = "tab:subregions", font_size = "scriptsize")
)
```

# Testing and Validation

## Stratigraphic Excavations and Radiocarbon Calibrations

The chronological architecture of the model relies on stratified excavations across key prehistoric and Early Historic settlements in Tamil Nadu and Kerala [@Rao1985Indian; @Thapar1979Indian; @Thapar1981Indian]. Radiocarbon determinations from multiple deep sounding sequences establish secure chronological baselines:
- Keeladi on the Vaigai River yielded AMS radiocarbon dates spanning from the sixth century BC (580BC) through the third century AD, establishing that literate urban society in southern Tamil Nadu emerged contemporary with the urbanisation of the Gangetic valley rather than as a secondary offshoot [@Baskar2026Regional; @Rao1985Indian].
- Kodumanal in the Kongu uplands produced stratified sequences showing continuous industrial occupation from the Iron Age Megalithic phase (ca. 500BC) through the Sangam climax (ca. 250AD), confirming prolonged craft specialisation in beryl, quartz, carnelian and high-carbon steel [@Abraham2003Chera].
- Pattanam on the Periyar delta in Kerala yielded charcoal and wood samples from wharf structures and occupational deposits with radiocarbon determinations clustering between 1000BC (Iron Age precursor horizon) and 400AD (Indo-Roman commercial zenith) [@Kelly2024Report].
- Adichanallur in the Thamirabarani valley yielded thermoluminescence and radiocarbon dates on funerary urns confirming intensive mortuary use between 1000BC and 600BC [@MushrifTripathy2019Tales].

## Archaeobotanical and Isotopic Subsistence Tracking

Archaeobotanical investigations confirm the dual agrarian foundation of southern peninsular societies [@Fuller2020Chapter; @KingwellBanham2019Rainfed; @Saraswat1991Archaeobot]. Flotation samples from Neolithic through Early Historic strata demonstrate that indigenous dry millets (*Brachiaria ramosa*, *Setaria verticillata*) and pulses (*Macrotyloma uniflorum*) sustained early population growth in the semi-arid interior tablelands [@Fuller2020Chapter].

During the first millennium BC, wet-rice agriculture (*Oryza sativa*) expanded rapidly across deltaic floodplains, accompanied by banana (*Musa*) cultivation and coconut arboriculture along the humid Malabar and Coromandel coasts [@Fuller2009Banana]. Weed flora analysis by Kingwell-Banham confirms that rice cultivation shifted from rainfed wetland foraging to systematically bunded, tank-irrigated paddy fields, enabling multiple annual harvests that generated the caloric surpluses necessary to support dense urban craft centres [@KingwellBanham2019Rainfed].

Bioarchaeological analysis of human skeletal series from Adichanallur, Korkai and Megalithic burial cists reveals low frequencies of cribra orbitalia and linear enamel hypoplasia compared to contemporary urban populations of the northern plains, reflecting a balanced nutritional regime incorporating animal protein, marine and riverine fish, millets and legumes [@MushrifTripathy2019Tales].

## Epigraphic and Numismatic Concordance

The transition to Early Historic urbanism is cross-checked through epigraphic and numismatic evidence [@Dwivedi2021Tools; @Dwivedi2019Early]. Over 110 rock shelters in Tamil Nadu contain Tamil-Brahmi donative inscriptions carved by merchant guilds, royal donors and lay devotees recording gifts of stone beds to Jain ascetics (*samana munivar*), confirming the spread of literacy and monastic networks along interior trade corridors between 300BC and 200AD [@Monsingh2025Ancient; @Selvakumar2018Paliyars].

Furthermore, excavations at Keeladi, Kodumanal, Alagankulam and Korkai yielded hundreds of potsherds bearing inscribed personal names in Tamil-Brahmi script (*Athan*, *Nedunchezhiyan*, *Kuviran*), demonstrating that literacy was not restricted to religious elites but extended to potters, craftspeople and merchants [@Baskar2026Regional; @Raja2026Tracing].

Numismatic finds provide independent geographical verification for commercial integration:
- Local punch-marked and cast copper coins issued by the Pandya (featuring fish emblems), Chera (bow and arrow emblems) and Chola (standing tiger emblems) kings circulate widely within their respective river basins [@Abraham2003Chera; @Dwivedi2021Political].
- Massive hoards of Roman gold aurei and silver denarii of Augustus, Tiberius, Caligula and Nero, found in dense clusters across the Coimbatore-Karur corridor and coastal Malabar (Kottayam, Eyyal), confirm high-volume trade in pepper, beryl and fine textiles [@Tomber2009Migration; @Cobb2023Indian].

## Asymptotic Saturation Audit

The INDUS source ledger for Tamil Nadu and Kerala was compiled through a four-wave asymptotic ingestion process to ensure geographical comprehensiveness:
- Wave 1: Ingestion of primary historical metropolis anchors, official national censuses (Census of India Table A-04) and historical gazetteers [@ImperialGazetteer1908; @Champakalakshmi1996Trade], contributing 916 catalogued settlements.
- Wave 2: Systematic audit of multi-repository archaeological corpora (ASI P1371, Pleiades, Zenodo IAR excavation series, Wikidata, OSM, XRONOS and c14bazAAR), adding 442 prehistoric and Early Historic sites.
- Wave 3: Macro-calibrated pre-1800 *qasba* and *nadu* continuity audit with foundation-year and chronological toponymy filtering, adding 221 settlements.
- Wave 4: Sub-mask gap sweeps and homonym audits across all three sub-regions, confirming 0 unaccounted settlements and verifying complete spatial saturation (marginal gain 0,0%).

In total, 1.762 candidate localities were audited: 1.579 were accepted as primary settlements (842 in Kaveri Delta and Tondaimandalam, 457 in the Vaigai-Thamirabarani Pandya heartland and 280 in Chera Malabar) and 183 were excluded or consolidated as duplicate aliases and post-domain foundations.

# Results

## Demographic Trajectory and Benchmark Analysis

The long-term population trajectory of Tamil Nadu and Kerala across ten millennia reveals a steady upward ascent characterised by two distinct accelerations: the Early Iron Age Megalithic expansion (1000BC to 500BC) and the Sangam trans-oceanic commercial climax (200BC to 300AD) (Figure \ref{fig:trajectory} and Table \ref{tab:benchmarks}).

```{r fig-trajectory, results='asis'}
viscount_figure(
  "figures/fig2_tamil_nadu_and_kerala_up_to_tamilakam_demography.png",
  "Long-term demographic trajectory of Tamil Nadu and Kerala (10000BC to 300AD), showing benchmark growth across three sub-regions, Sangam urban florescence and Zipf rank-size distribution ($\\alpha = 0,94$, $R^2 = 0,95$) across 1.579 settlements.",
  "fig:trajectory"
)
```

```{r tbl-benchmarks, results='asis'}
bm_years <- c("-10000", "-5000", "-2000", "-1000", "-500", "-200", "0", "200", "300")
bm_rows <- lapply(bm_years, function (yk) {
  tot_pop <- as.numeric(mod_data$summary$headline_population_by_benchmark[[yk]])
  cher <- as.numeric(mod_data$regions$tam1_chera_malabar$population[[yk]])
  chol <- as.numeric(mod_data$regions$tam1_chola_kaveri$population[[yk]])
  pand <- as.numeric(mod_data$regions$tam1_pandya_vaigai$population[[yk]])
  dens <- tot_pop / tot_area * 100
  data.frame(
    Benchmark = fmt_yr(yk),
    RegionalPop = viscount_fmt_pop(tot_pop),
    Density = viscount_fmt_number(dens, 2L),
    KaveriDelta = viscount_fmt_pop(chol),
    PandyaHeartland = viscount_fmt_pop(pand),
    CheraMalabar = viscount_fmt_pop(cher),
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE
  )
})
df_bm <- do.call(rbind, bm_rows)
viscount_table(
  df_bm,
  "Benchmark population totals and sub-regional distribution across Tamil Nadu and Kerala (10000BC to 300AD).",
  c("Benchmark", "Regional Pop", "Density", "Kaveri Delta", "Pandya Heartland", "Chera Malabar"),
  list(label = "tab:benchmarks", font_size = "scriptsize")
)
```

## Four Historical Demographic Epochs

### Terminal Pleistocene and Early Holocene Foraging (10000BC to 5000BC)

During the terminal Pleistocene and early Holocene, the southern tip of India accommodated sparse, highly mobile bands of microlithic foragers. Regional population grew from 35k in 10000BC (density: 20,90 persons per 100 km²) to 120k in 5000BC (71,66 persons per 100 km²). Settlement was concentrated along coastal dune belts (*teri* formations) in the south, river terrace bluffs along the Kortallaiyar and Palar in the north, and upland rock shelters in the Western Ghats [@Biswas2022Founder; @Tacon2010Rock]. Communities subsisted on small-game hunting, wild vegetable foraging and coastal mollusc collecting, maintaining small, ephemeral camps [@Rick2022Coring; @Das2016Tracing].

### Southern Neolithic and Early Pastoral Development (5000BC to 1000BC)

Between 5000BC and 1000BC, food-producing adaptations spread into the northern interior plateaus and foothill valleys. Population reached 480k in 2000BC (286,64 persons per 100 km²) and climbed to 1,15M by 1000BC (686,74 persons per 100 km²). Pastoral cattle camps with ash-mounds appeared in Dharmapuri and Krishnagiri, complemented by sedentary villages cultivating indigenous millets and horsegram [@Roberts2015Local; @Saraswat1991Archaeobot; @Fuller2020Chapter]. In the Western Ghats and coastal Malabar, arboriculture and yam harvesting deepened, while exchange in lithic raw materials linked upland communities with coastal foragers [@Selvakumar2018Paliyars; @Kelly2024Report].

### Iron Age Megalithic Expansion and Proto-Urban Coalescence (1000BC to 200BC)

The introduction of iron metallurgy after 1000BC triggered an agricultural and demographic revolution [@K2014Early; @Rao1989South]. Population expanded from 1,15M in 1000BC to 2,10M in 500BC (1.254,05 persons per 100 km²) and 3,40M by 200BC (2.030,36 persons per 100 km²).

This epoch was distinguished by:
1. Construction of extensive earthen irrigation tanks across the Vaigai, Thamirabarani and Kaveri drainage systems, facilitating wet-rice cultivation and insulating agriculturalists against drought [@KingwellBanham2019Rainfed].
2. Ubiquitous construction of megalithic monuments, indicating expanding population densities and collective lineage organisation [@Rao1989South; @Wunderlich2019Hierarchy].
3. Emergence of specialised pyrotechnological craft centres, such as Kodumanal for steel production and gem cutting [@Abraham2003Chera; @Kelly2024Report].
4. Nucleation of early civic capitals at Madurai on the Vaigai, Uraiyur on the Kaveri, and Kanchipuram on the Palar, laying the groundwork for classical Sangam urbanisation [@Baskar2026Regional; @Dwivedi2019Early].

### Sangam Urban Florescence and Indo-Roman Climax (200BC to 300AD)

Between 200BC and 300AD, Tamilakam reached its classical peak of cultural, political and economic development [@Monsingh2025Ancient; @Abraham2003Chera]. Regional population increased from 3,40M in 200BC to 4,20M in 0AD (2.508,10 persons per 100 km²), 4,80M in 200AD and 5,10M by 300AD (3.045,54 persons per 100 km²).

This urban climax was characterised by:
- Growth of primary metropolises: Madurai (48k peak in 100AD; 42,7k in 0AD), Kaveripattinam (45k peak in 200AD; 34,3k in 0AD), Kanchipuram (42,7k peak in 300AD; 30k in 0AD), Tiruchirappalli/Uraiyur (36k peak in 200AD; 32k in 0AD) and Pattanam/Muziris (36k peak in 100AD; 28k in 0AD).
- Development of specialised maritime emporia and secondary centres: Arikamedu (24k peak in 100AD; 20k in 0AD), Korkai (22k peak in 100AD; 19,8k in 0AD), Mylapore (13,7k peak in 300AD), Keeladi (11k peak in 100BC) and Alagankulam (4,3k in 300AD), funnelling pearls, pepper, beryl and cotton textiles into the Indian Ocean maritime trade network [@Tomber2009Migration; @Cobb2023Indian; @Abraham2023Recent].
- Dense rural infill across the Kaveri delta and Thamirabarani valley, where double-cropped paddy agriculture sustained local densities exceeding 3.500 persons per 100 km².
- Deepening institutionalisation of craft guilds, merchant corporations (*nanadesi*, *manigramam* precursors) and royal port customs administrations (*ayam*) [@Dwivedi2021Tools; @Dwivedi2021Political].

## Urban Hierarchy and Settlement Systems

Table \ref{tab:leading_settlements} presents the leading fifteen catalogued settlements across Tamil Nadu and Kerala ordered by peak population.

```{r tbl-leading-settlements, results='asis'}
set_list <- unname(set_data)
sett_peaks <- vapply(set_list, function (s) {
  if (is.null(s$population) || length(s$population) == 0) return(0)
  max(as.numeric(unlist(s$population)))
}, numeric(1))

ord <- order(sett_peaks, decreasing = TRUE)
top_sett <- set_list[ord]

top_rows <- lapply(head(top_sett, 15), function (s) {
  p_max <- max(as.numeric(unlist(s$population)))
  p_0 <- if (!is.null(s$population[["0"]])) as.numeric(s$population[["0"]]) else "-"
  lat <- as.numeric(s$coords[[1]])
  lon <- as.numeric(s$coords[[2]])
  coord_str <- paste0(viscount_fmt_number(abs(lat), 2L), if (lat >= 0) " N" else " S", ", ",
                      viscount_fmt_number(abs(lon), 2L), if (lon >= 0) " E" else " W")
  rk_s <- if (!is.null(s$region_id)) s$region_id else s$region
  reg_lbl <- if (!is.null(reg_short[[rk_s]])) reg_short[[rk_s]] else clean_text(s$region)
  data.frame(
    Name = clean_text(s$name),
    SubRegion = reg_lbl,
    Coordinates = coord_str,
    PeakPop = viscount_fmt_pop(p_max),
    P0AD = if (is.numeric(p_0)) viscount_fmt_pop(p_0) else "-",
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE
  )
})
df_top <- do.call(rbind, top_rows)
viscount_table(
  df_top,
  "Leading fifteen prehistoric and Early Historic settlements in Tamil Nadu and Kerala, showing coordinates, peak population and 0AD population.",
  c("Settlement Name", "Sub-Region", "Coordinates", "Peak Pop", "0AD Pop"),
  list(label = "tab:leading_settlements", font_size = "scriptsize")
)
```

Evaluated across all 1.579 catalogued settlements, the urban hierarchy conforms to a Zipf rank-size distribution ($\alpha = 0,94$, $R^2 = 0,95$) [@Erdosy1988Urbanisation; @Champakalakshmi1996Trade] and displays a structured four-tiered configuration:
1. Primary metropolitan capitals (> 30k peak inhabitants): Madurai (48k peak in 100AD), Kaveripattinam/Puhar (45k in 200AD), Kanchipuram (42,7k in 300AD), Tiruchirappalli/Uraiyur (36k in 200AD) and Pattanam/Muziris (36k in 100AD). These centres operated as political capitals, major craft manufacturing nodes and trans-oceanic maritime gateways.
2. Major regional centres and emporia (10k to 25k peak inhabitants): Arikamedu/Poduke (24k peak in 100AD), Korkai (22k in 100AD), Mylapore (13,7k in 300AD), Tondaimandalam nodal towns such as Ambattur (12,9k), Poonamallee (12,9k), Sholinganallur (12,8k), Tambaram (12,5k) and Alandur (12,1k), alongside Kalkulam (11,3k) and Keeladi (11k peak in 100BC). These settlements commanded trade routes across the Bay of Bengal, the Palk Strait and the Gulf of Mannar.
3. Secondary manufacturing and nodal towns (4k to 10k peak inhabitants): Cuddalore (9,7k in 300AD), Kanayannur (9,5k), Vadakara (9,4k), Tirurangadi (9,3k), Tirur (9,3k), Kakinada (9k), Kodumanal (9k peak in 100BC), Palakkad (7,5k), Valparai (6,4k), Alagankulam (4,3k) and Karur (4,1k). These towns coordinated gem production, iron smelting, pearl processing and regional agrarian exchange.
4. Tertiary market villages and agricultural hamlets (< 4k peak inhabitants): Kunnukara (3k peak in 600BC), Thuraiyur (2,5k in 300AD), Rameswaram (1,2k in 300AD), Adichanallur (1k in 300AD) and over 1.500 smaller market and agrarian settlements distributed across the river valleys and coastal plains.

# Limitations

Archaeological visibility and demographic reconstruction in southern peninsular India are shaped by specific environmental and taphonomic factors:
1. Soil chemistry and organic preservation: the acidic lateritic soils of Kerala and tropical red soils of Tamil Nadu accelerate the decomposition of unburnt bone, wood, textiles and botanical remains, biasing the archaeological record toward durable materials such as ceramics, stone beads, iron slag and brick masonry [@MushrifTripathy2019Tales; @Kelly2024Report].
2. Coastal geomorphology and marine inundation: coastal progradation, lagoon siltation and historical storm surges have altered ancient harbour geographies. Ancient Puhar (Kaveripattinam) suffered marine transgression and estuarine shifting, Korkai is now situated several kilometres inland from the modern shoreline due to deltaic siltation of the Thamirabarani, and the exact contours of Muziris at Pattanam were obscured by Periyar flood silts [@Tomber2009Migration; @Abraham2023Recent].
3. Urban continuity and modern overbuilding: major historic centres such as Madurai, Tiruchirappalli (Uraiyur), Kanchipuram and Karur have experienced continuous human occupation for over two millennia, severely restricting large-scale horizontal excavations beneath densely populated modern urban fabrics [@Abraham2003Chera; @Rao1985Indian].
4. Epigraphic bias toward elite donative contexts: early inscriptions on stone beds and cave walls predominantly record religious donations by merchant elites and royal patrons, leaving lower-status rural cultivators and unenslaved agricultural labourers less visible in the textual record [@Dwivedi2021Political; @Monsingh2025Ancient].

# Conclusion

The long-term demographic development of Tamil Nadu and Kerala from 10000BC to 300AD reveals the gradual emergence of a densely settled, technologically sophisticated and cosmopolitan civilisational domain in southern peninsular India. Expanding from 35k terminal Pleistocene foragers in 10000BC, regional population climbed through the Southern Neolithic and Early Iron Age Megalithic transitions to reach 1,15M in 1000BC and 2,10M in 500BC, culminating in a classical Sangam population of 5,10M in 300AD across 167.458 km² of territory.

This demographic growth was propelled by the expansion of tank-irrigated wet-rice agriculture in the fertile Kaveri, Vaigai and Thamirabarani river valleys, the development of specialised iron and steel pyrotechnology in the Kongu uplands, and the flowering of trans-oceanic maritime commerce connecting the Malabar and Coromandel coasts with Rome, the Red Sea and Southeast Asia. Far from being a peripheral appendage to northern Indian polities, Sangam Tamilakam developed an autonomous urban culture characterised by civic planning, active craft guilds, widespread literacy in Tamil-Brahmi script and an integrated commercial hierarchy that laid the foundations for the mediaeval South Indian kingdoms [@Champakalakshmi1996Trade; @Chattopadhyaya1994Making].

# Appendix

The INDUS source ledger for Tamil Nadu and Kerala reconciles 1.579 catalogued settlements across three sub-regions (842 in Kaveri Delta and Tondaimandalam, 457 in the Vaigai-Thamirabarani Pandya heartland and 280 in Chera Malabar) against 1.762 candidate entries and 183 documented exclusions. Table \ref{tab:saturation} details the four-wave saturation audit demonstrating comprehensive regional coverage.

```{r tbl-saturation, results='asis'}
sat_waves <- led_data$saturation_audit$waves
sat_rows <- lapply(sat_waves, function (w) {
  data.frame(
    Wave = paste0("Wave ", w$wave),
    SourceClass = clean_text(w$source_class),
    PriorTotal = viscount_fmt_number(as.numeric(w$prior_cumulative_included), 0L),
    NewlyIncluded = viscount_fmt_number(as.numeric(w$newly_included), 0L),
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE
  )
})
df_sat <- do.call(rbind, sat_rows)
viscount_table(
  df_sat,
  "Four-wave asymptotic saturation audit of catalogued settlements across Tamil Nadu and Kerala.",
  c("Ingestion Wave", "Source Category", "Prior Cumulative", "Newly Included"),
  list(label = "tab:saturation", font_size = "scriptsize")
)
```
